sections.h2: How the tax bill is figured
sections.html:
Your property's assessed market value is the starting number. A state rate converts it to taxable value, and the local levy turns that into general tax by multiplying taxable value by mills and dividing by 1,000. One mill means $1 of tax on each $1,000 of taxable value. Your appraisal notice lists last year's total mills set by the taxing bodies where you live.

General tax is not always the whole bill. Charges for solid waste, street lighting and special or rural improvement districts can ride along, and the county treasurer will explain any line you do not recognize.

A higher value on your notice does not mean a matching jump in tax, since rates and levies move as well. The 2025 to 2026 appraisal cycle values property as of January 1, 2024. The previous cycle covered 2023 to 2024, with a January 1, 2022 value date. Expect the bill in late October. A seller should open it right away, because its due dates shape the closing.

MCA 15-16-102 splits the year's tax into two payments. November 30 at 5 p.m. is the first deadline, extended to 30 days after postmark if the notice went out late. May 31 at 5 p.m. is the second. If either lands on a Saturday or holiday, you have until 5 p.m. the next business day, free of penalty and interest.

Tax left unpaid turns delinquent. Interest of 5/6 of 1% builds each month it stays open, and a flat 2% penalty is added. Paying the current year without the delinquent years is allowed. Money aimed at delinquent taxes, though, is credited to the oldest year first.

Owners of a primary residence can spread the bill out. Seven equal payments, each one-seventh of the total, fall on these dates: November 30, December 31, January 31, February 28, March 31, April 30 and May 31. Miss one and the normal interest and penalty apply.

  • Read the bill ahead of closing so the title company can quote an exact payoff.
  • Ask the treasurer whether special assessments are included.
  • Find out if the house is enrolled for a reduced rate rather than assuming the standard one.

Use decides the rate. For 2026, a qualifying owner-occupied home or long-term rental is taxed on a sliding scale that opens at 0.76%. A second home, short-term rental or vacant residential lot is charged one flat 1.90%.

Farm and forest parcels with a house are split. The house and its one-acre homesite get the sliding residential scale when the owner lives there or rents it long term. If the house is a second home or short-term rental, the rate is 1.90% on non-qualified agricultural and forest parcels and 1.35% on qualified agricultural ones. A parcel of 160 or more acres counts as agricultural on its own, and a smaller one has to show agricultural use and income.

Two reduced rates carry most of the relief. The Homestead Reduced Rate covers the owner's own principal residence. The Long-Term Rental Reduced Rate covers a home leased out in stays of 28 days or more for at least seven months. Enrollment goes through the Department of Revenue. The window for 2027 opened May 4, 2026 and closes March 1, 2027, and the department matches enrollment to the property geocode.

A lien notice from the county treasurer has to list the help on offer under MCA 15-17-125: the homestead reduced tax rate, the rental property reduced tax rate, state property tax assistance, and the residential property tax credit for the elderly.

Eligibility, enrollment and what happens when you sell are laid out in our Montana homestead exemption guide. Struggling with a bill? Raise these programs with the treasurer or the Department of Revenue early, ahead of any lien.

Real property taxes that remain delinquent lead to a lien, attached by the county treasurer by the first working day in August at the latest. Proper notice is a condition. The county keeps the lien unless it assigns it to a third party, and where notice was defective no lien may attach (MCA 15-17-125).

A mailed warning has to go out two weeks or more before attachment. Once the lien is on, the treasurer signs a tax lien certificate, files a copy with the clerk and recorder, and mails another to the person assessed.

  • The certificate gives the delinquency date and the date the lien attached.
  • Tax, penalties, interest and costs are itemized separately.
  • It cautions that a tax deed may follow and states the date the county or an assignee can claim one.

Counties post their own cutoff dates inside that framework, so phone your treasurer for this year's lien date. The tax deed step comes later, with a notice window of May 1 to May 30 in the redemption year. A sale that closes before the lien attaches keeps the payoff simple.

Get a current payoff from the county treasurer and let the closing statement settle it. Delinquent bills, lien certificates and even a running tax deed clock do not stop a sale. The balance is paid from the proceeds, and the title company requires that.

Before fixing a closing date:

  • Check the appraisal notice for the classification and value the Department of Revenue assigned.
  • See whether the reduced rate is active, since it ends at year end after a sale.
  • Ask the treasurer about earlier-year delinquency, penalties and interest.
  • If the value looks wrong, use the review deadline printed on the notice.

Behind on taxes? Cash Home Buyers can make an as-is cash offer, and since the title company pays the balance out of the proceeds at closing, you need not raise the money first. Nothing here is legal or tax advice. Exact figures come from the county treasurer or the Department of Revenue.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Montana?
faqs.a: The first half is due November 30 (5 p.m.), or 30 days after the notice postmark if that is later. The second half is due May 31 (5 p.m.). Bills usually arrive in late October.

faqs.q: What is the penalty for late Montana property tax?
faqs.a: Interest of 5/6 of 1% per month runs on delinquent tax until it is paid, and a 2% penalty is added on top (MCA 15-16-102).

faqs.q: Can I pay Montana property tax monthly?
faqs.a: Yes, for a primary residence. Seven installments are due on the last day of each month from November 30 through May 31, and a missed one brings interest and penalty.

faqs.q: What is the Montana property tax rate on a second home in 2026?
faqs.a: 1.90% flat. Short-term rentals and vacant residential lots pay the same.

faqs.q: When does Montana attach a tax lien?
faqs.a: By the first working day in August, following a mailed notice at least two weeks earlier (MCA 15-17-125).
